Interviewer:	I’ve just got a few questions about how the placement’s going and how it relates to your course and things like that, OK?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	When did you start on the placement?

Subject:	I started the 3rd of August.

Interviewer:	It’s been going quite a while now then?

Subject:	Six months.

Interviewer:	OK. Can you tell me a bit about [company] and what they do?

Subject:	 [Company] is a multi-discipline engineering firm and they do transport, they do structural work, they do rail work, and geotechnics. They’ve got quite a few office in, elsewhere in UK and overseas.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	It’s quite, um, open support – people are quite supportive and they’re willing to help you and share their experiences. That could be, um, different in different teams. I’m quite lucky that I worked in a team that people are really nice and friendly. Um, [company] got 12 key indicators and five, I don’t know what it’s called, five something that is customer obsessions, um, innovative, something, something. It basically tells you what the company wants you to achieve and everything, you know, it sounds like a promoter now. Um, yeah, it’s – they are quite focussed on customers. (Right, OK) I understand why, and they’ve got quite a few courses that they would like us to go on if we want to. They are always putting a huge amount of budget for training.

Interviewer:	OK. How useful do you think that the work that you’ve done on your degree has been to the work that you’re doing now?

Subject:	I’d say 90% not relevant.

Interviewer:	Not relevant?

Subject:	Because I’m doing transport, which is something that I didn’t expect that I would do. (Right) Um, um, what is useful that I’ve done in [university], it’s the way to approach the work and the way to analyse things. Um, so far what I’ve done is not very technical and I didn’t do any transport modules in [university], that’s why it’s not relevant.

Interviewer:	OK. Is there anything that you wished you had learnt before you started the placement? Do you wish now that you had done transport modules or doesn’t it matter…?

Subject:	Um, well, it probably would be nice if I had, but I’d presume what you’ve learned in uni, it’s just a base to provide you with what, learning more actual practical knowledge. Um, so I think it’s OK that I didn’t do any transport.

Interviewer:	OK, were you taught anything about health and safety at university?

Subject:	Um, it’s been highlighted when I was in uni but there wasn’t a specific course or guidelines because that varies from companies to companies, but they did make us know how important it is.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so have you had health and safety training when you arrived here?

Subject:	Oh loads. Probably every – when I first started – probably every week, or there was a few courses in the same week, before they can let us go on site and do anything.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for coming on placement?

Subject:	Well it’s hard for me to say, because this is the only company that I have been working with. They’ve got guidelines of how to park in highways and everything. They could be different from other companies. So I think uni has done enough to make us know how important it is.

Interviewer:	OK, before you started on placement did the university or your department say what they hoped you’d get out of doing a placement?

Subject:	They just said, make myself enjoy what I’m doing and, yeah, just an experience that, you know, the students who didn’t go on the placement wouldn’t get.

Interviewer:	OK, how have you found the transition from education to work, is it really easy or difficult?

Subject:	Um, I wouldn’t say difficult but certainly it’s very different. (Yes) Yeah. Um, there’s – every day I have to go to work and there’s no day off on Wednesdays. (OK) And, um, especially when I’m in traffic, I have to deal with the clients, authorities, myself, um, it’s not awfully technical but it could be quite difficult, and that’s not what we learned from uni. That’s real life and – yeah, real world.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you could have learned more inter-personal skills at uni or do you think it’s something that you develop through experience and that’s why doing a placement is a good idea?

Subject:	Mm, I’d think that’d be learned as you work, because uni gives you a chance to do it but it would be different, they couldn’t pretend that they are clients and start shouting at you. (Yeah) Because people in uni are always nice and chilled out and relaxed and it’s not about profit and, and deadline and everything, so, yeah, it’s two different situations.

Interviewer:	OK. How do you think work and university do differ then? What do you think are the main differences?

Subject:	Um, in uni we work and it’s about, we are going to, um, achieve a 2:1 or first grade and we are – as long as we’ve got the work done we can chill out and relax and do whatever we want. Um, well although we shouldn’t but I assume everybody did skip classes, well you can’t really do that at work and there’s more responsibility when you’re at work because you are issuing something, you are designing something, and people could have had a hard time if you’ve got a bad design and you could get yourself into troubles.

Interviewer:	Do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d say so. University, it’s more a short term goal, you can see yourself finishing in three, four, five years, but at work, that doesn’t get you a long way. If you are good and bright and you’ve got chances, probably five years you could be a manager but you can’t really vision the whole path.

Interviewer:	OK. What area are you working in here, is it transport?

Subject:	Transport planning.

Interviewer:	OK. Are there many women in your team?

Subject:	Both. Um, when I first started there was about eight men and three women including me. (OK) And now we’ve got five women, less male.

Interviewer:	OK. Does the company have a structure or a programme in place for placement students to follow?

Subject:	Mm, what do you mean by that?

Interviewer:	Maybe with specific targets and things that you should achieve throughout the year that you’re here?

Subject:	No, not really, but they tend to provide you some help with your final year project and year out report. (OK) And they have, well we have appraisals, like other employees.

Interviewer:	So, you kind of have a scheme but it’s something everyone in the whole company does?

Subject:	I’ve heard that they’ve got sponsorships and other things but my manager didn’t mention it to me, so I don’t know if it varies from teams to teams or just my manager didn’t want to tell me.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that it’d be a good idea if you had a specific programme to follow while you were here, or are you happy with the way things are going and what you’re doing at the minute?

Subject:	It could be nice if there was a programme. Sometimes I feel that I’d like to have more feedbacks to know how I’m doing because I’m so new, and I don’t know what sort of work I should get out of it, um, and I’m quite lack of experiences because I’m totally new to transport. Um, yeah.

Interviewer:	What does your actual job role involve then?

Subject:	Um, in transport planning there are safety studies, economic schemes, um, general planning, um, I’ve been working on safer routes to school, um, a safety scheme that is [motorway] Junction 18, um, I’ve been helping with [name] County Council it’s something about designing the pedestrian path for the whole area and I’m working on regional freight network, the south west, now.

Interviewer:	OK, is that what you expected to be doing or were told to expect before you started?

Subject:	Mm. I was told that I would go out on sites probably once every week and now it depends, sometimes I got on site a few days in a row, sometimes I don’t get out in a whole month. It’s quite, well I’d say different, though I didn’t have a lot of expectation when I first started, again because I didn’t know what transport really is. It’s, um, I know that when, probably when you have more experience you’ll get to use the technical software like (Quadrow?) or (Oskadee?) and do safety schemes, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been given the right level of responsibility?

Subject:	Mm. I was chatting to a girl in my group. She used to work like a summer placement in the other office in [company] and she thinks that I have a lot more responsibility than she did, which is good.

Interviewer:	Yes, OK, but even though you think you’ve got the right level of responsibility, do you feel that your team are supportive of you and if you do need help or anything?

Subject:	Extremely supportive, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. How would you summarise your placement experience so far?

Subject:	Um, there are ups and downs. Um, you feel quite good when you see a report issued with your name on it, but then you feel, oh, will they come back to me? And it’s – sometimes clients and the Government give you quite a hard time and they don’t, they could be fed up with work so they don’t speak really nicely and, yeah, but it’s a good experience that I know what the real world is and if I want to stay and work in England after I’ve graduated.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that you will want to stay here when you’ve graduated?

Subject:	In [company] or in England?

Interviewer:	Both.

Subject:	Well, yes and no. I like the company, I like my team, but I’m not sure if transport is the right career for me. (OK) Sometimes I do still fancy working in structural, but on the other hand it seems quite boring in structural because for the whole, I don’t know, three, four or five months you’re calculating the same bridge or same project, but with transport you jump from here to there.

Interviewer:	It’s more varied?

Subject:	You have different projects going on at the same time. So I might go and try out in structural later in April and see what I like.

Interviewer:	So, within [company] they would maybe let you have that opportunity to …?

Subject:	Yeah, possibly go to the other floors and I’ll stay there for a few weeks.

Interviewer:	Yes, that’s good.

Subject:	Yeah. Um, as for England I don’t really know. It’s too expensive and engineering doesn’t give you what you’re worth. You work hard, you’ve got a lot of responsibility, you’ve got a lot to take from the clients and everyone, you’ve got a lot of work, but they don’t give you enough money and the taxes are quite heavy as well. (Yes) So it all depends on what the company offers me and I’ll also check the salaries for engineering in other countries.

Interviewer:	So do you think that’s the biggest factor when you decide where to work or who is offering you the best package as it were rather than, I definitely want to go to this country or I definitely want to go to that country?

Subject:	Um, both of them are important reasons. While they are offering you something, it could be – it depends on, oh how shall I explain it? They might offer you less but the cost of living there and having a better standard of life could be cheaper, so it depends. And there are some countries that I wouldn’t want to go, and also I, I’m planning to go to a country and stay there for a few years and then change to another, so …

Interviewer:	So you’d like to travel about?

Subject:	Yeah, and that’s why I chose engineering.

Interviewer:	Yes, because it’s something you can do everywhere?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s not similar to law or something like that that you have to stay.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that everything about doing a placement is good, or do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement at all?

Subject:	Um, in which aspect? Like drawback as in the fantasy is broken, or if I would do it again, or?

Interviewer:	Would you recommend that other people do a placement?

Subject:	Yeah I would. Um, you will be more competitive when you graduate and you could have contacts with companies and people, and you are not – you would be more, um, close to the real world. You are prepared for what you’re going to do when you’ve graduated.
Interviewer:	Yes, they’re all the positive things. Do you think there are many disadvantages to doing a placement?

Subject:	At the moment not really. Sometimes they tend to give me some easier work but I think no matter – probably because I’m placement or because I’ve no experience, so I think even though you’re a graduate, when you have no experience they’ll do the same. (OK) Oh, the only drawback is the salary. (Yes) It’s really, really bad!

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that you have changed from doing the placement?

Subject:	Lots. Um, when I was in uni I thought I would like to do the MEng and I would like to work in the UK, and I wouldn’t mind to go to work on site. And I was only going to be either site engineer or structural engineer, and I thought I would choose no other career other than engineering, but now I’m not, I’m not sure if I will stay, if I will be site engineering, if I will stick with engineering.

Interviewer:	So you think there’s a possibility you might do something completely different?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s possible.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think you’ll use what you’re learning now when you go back to your final year?

Subject:	Yeah, I will. Um, in – study-wise there’s a module about highways that I think I should be more, having advantage over other course-mates, and my Excel skills that I learned here and, yeah, the way to organise things.

Interviewer:	OK. I know [name] is here but are there any other placement students at [company]?

Subject:	Yeah, there are two other on my floor. One of them is from [university] as well and he, he was doing transport modules but he doesn’t work in transport planning, he works in [name]. I think that’s something to do with management. The other girl is, um, in the other team doing, oh I forgot what she does, but she did geography.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that it’s an advantage or a disadvantage having other placement students here, or don’t you have much to do with them?

Subject:	I don’t have much to do with them. Mm. I just see them as other colleagues. (Yes) That, um, that’s as junior as I am.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel like you’re all treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

Subject:	I think so, yeah. Yeah. Sometimes we might have less chances to go on training courses because we are not (inaudible). I’ve been told that some of them couldn’t go on training courses because they are not permanent employee.

Interviewer:	OK, Is most of your work done in teams, or are you working a lot on your own?

Subject:	I work quite a lot on my own, but because what I – for the current project that I’m doing it’s a project given to my colleague and he gave it to me, so whenever I’ve got problems I go back to him. That makes like a group work. And when we go out on sites normally we go out in pairs.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that doing teamwork at work compares to doing teamwork at university?

Subject:	Um, in uni some of your course-mates can get quite irresponsible. I’m not saying my course because people in my course work fine, but when we work with some other courses, yeah. In here, um, they are quite determined and they are quite willing to, um, give the best output, so that’s something in common. And the group work in uni it’s – you tend to have the ideal situation, that something always works out, but in the real world there are more other factors that stops you and slow you down, and sometimes you, when you want to try to get some information, the other societies or parties will stop you or slow you down. So it’s not as fast as doing group work in uni.

Interviewer:	Do you think that in the workplace individuals in a team maybe have a clearer role of what their job is than at uni?

Subject:	Mm, possibly, yeah. Because again in uni when your group-mates don’t want to work, you’ve got to do what they want to do. Otherwise you just have a bad grade or, yeah, but in a company since all of them are quite willing to do something and they know what their role is, they know that if they don’t – response – they are not responsible for what they’re doing they’ll get into trouble as well.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Do you think that it’s worthwhile doing teamwork at university? Even though it’s different to teamwork in the workplace, do you think that you still learn things from it?

Subject:	Yeah. One of the reasons is there will be too much work if you work on your own, and it’s inter-personal skills that you get out of it from group work and you get to know your course-mate better as well.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. At work are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	Yeah, there are. They are nice people but they are just perfectionalist, it’s too hard to work with.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Have you been given a mentor at all?

Subject:	Not really, um, I’ve heard that a girl who is on placement as well, not from my floor, she has like a mentor, but we – well I just go and say something that I don’t like or like to my manager when I need, but he’s too busy, so I don’t always have the chance.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’d be a good idea to have a mentor then?

Subject:	Mm, it might. It is not that only me who don’t have a mentor but I don’t think anybody in our team has a mentor.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think would be the benefits of having a mentor?

Subject:	Mm, I could discuss more openly about, well, the packages or the possibilities of coming back after I graduate. Um, I’d say the career-wise would be clearer.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there would be any drawbacks to having a mentor, or disadvantages?

Subject:	I’m not sure because I don’t have one.

Interviewer:	OK. Is there anyone else apart from your line manager that you’ll go to for advice at all?

Subject:	Yeah, my, my seniors. There are two, who are project managers, and one of them did my appraisal, so I’ll go and ask something if I want to know, but because he’s not yet a manager there are things that he doesn’t know yet.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Is there anyone else in the company that you think of as a role model?

Subject:	As a role model?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	In the company? My, um – the boss on my floor. He says that it was, there was a ball for the company and we were chatting, he said oh those few are star graduates, and my line manager thinks everybody in our team are outstanding, so I think basically everybody is doing a good job. And I know that my line manager’s quite hard-working and I look up to him, but I wouldn’t think that I would be as committed as he is.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that?

Subject:	Because I wouldn’t come in the office from half seven and leave at half six!

Interviewer:	That’s like me! Has anyone from uni been to visit you?

Subject:	Yeah – er, it’s [name of placement tutor].

Interviewer:	OK. Did you know him before?

Subject:	Yeah, he did, um, surveying in my second year. 

Interviewer:	Did he tell you why he was visiting?

Subject:	Yes. Because he was around [town]. That’s why.

Interviewer:	OK, did he talk to you and your manager?

Subject:	Yes. Well my manager was quite busy so they had a brief chat. (Right) And me – it was quite a long chat and because I knew him before, apart from what’s supposed to be passed on to me, we did some chit-chat and…

Interviewer:	What sort of things was he asking you about the placement?

Subject:	He asked if everything’s going OK, um, and I just start telling him what I was doing, how I found this company, and he asked me what’s my career plan, my – the plan for my final year project and year out project, if I was planning to be chartered, what should I put in the portfolio, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Would you be happy to go to him if you had a problem with your placement?

Subject:	Yeah I would.

Interviewer:	Are you in contact with him or anyone else at uni the rest of the time?

Subject:	Mm, not on a regular basis, but I do contact him a few times and the other tutor, [name], um, it was about the summer placement that I asked him and sometimes I contact with my friends in [university] but that’s not relevant really.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know if either the university or here have a complaints procedure in place in case you did have any problems?

Subject:	Well let me think. I don’t know about it in [university]. Here … we have the foreman ask us if we know about it, but we don’t.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Oh yeah.

Interviewer:	What about when you go out on site?

Subject:	Well that’s not enough facilities for both male and female really. They just stop along a trunk road, so yeah. But most of the time they’ve got things that we need.

Interviewer:	And are there always women’s toilets on site and things like that?

Subject:	No, not really, but not for men either. (OK) So yeah.

Interviewer:	And what about safety clothing and things like that, does that fit you or is it all in men’s sizes?

Subject:	Well I’m happy because I’m not too small that I can fit in them. But I think [name] has a problem. They just don’t do smaller sizes in general. I think they can find it, but it’s just harder.

Interviewer:	OK. Can you think of any occasions when you feel like your gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people or the outcome of events?

Subject:	Mm. Not really. I’d say because transport is not as hard core as structural, so – and they are not expecting there’s only male colleagues, so you get – you don’t really have the problem. And I’ve never heard [name] saying that she has a problem, so I suppose a consultancy would be more open.

Interviewer:	Yeah OK. Do you feel the same about that when you go on site as well?

Subject:	Yeah, because it’s me and my colleague. (Yeah) So they, they know me well and I know them well, and we work happily together.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you have to deal with the labourers or anything like that at all?

Subject:	Um, sometimes, not really. We might go and ask them a few questions, that’s not really labourers but they are someone who’s responsible for the local (inaudible) that’s going up and down on a road, even though it wasn’t me who was chatting to him it was my colleague, so I don’t feel any, like, discrimination.

Interviewer:	OK that’s good. We spoke earlier about your career and you thought that you don’t know whether you definitely want to go into engineering or not. Why do you think that you are considering not going into engineering?

Subject:	It’s again salary. (Yeah) Um, I was thinking, if I stay in England I might consider alternatives, or might – it could be other companies. I’m not sure how much in general this career is offering, but sometimes I feel like I should get more for what I do.

Interviewer:	Have you thought about what you might do instead?

Subject:	Accounting. Yeah, possible. Or go into Government.

Interviewer:	OK. If you did stay in engineering, do you think that you’d like a more managerial role or would you like to go down the technical or specialist route?

Subject:	I used to think that I would be working in management side, but from seeing what my managers do I don’t think that’s very interesting. He has meetings, actual, actually every day, or sometimes two or three meetings in a day, and when I say sometimes customers or clients shout at us, I think he got even more than we do because he’s dealing with all of them.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed from doing the placement?

Subject:	Oh yeah, lots. Um, as I said I used to have all the goals that I thought I would like to achieve. Now I would think again and some of them has changed.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the placement will help you when you do start work? Even if you go into something completely different do you think the experience will still be helpful?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it would. There was, um, someone who came for an interview and she is a Masters student but because she has no, um, experience, I’m not sure if they’re going to take her but it sounds not very, um, it’s not someone that they would like to have, with no experience. And again, if I go into different fields, there are skills that I learned here that will, that could be applied there and wouldn’t learn there.

Interviewer:	Yeah – things like dealing with clients and things like that?

Subject:	Mm.

Interviewer:	OK, if [company] offered you a job, would you come and work for them when you’ve finished uni?

Subject:	Possibly, it depends on how much they are offering. I need to talk about money now! There was once – I went to a career fair, it was a few months ago in [airport], and I had a chat with the IStructE, the executive, and I can’t remember what he was but I think he’s the chief executive of IStructE, and I asked him about the salary, before and after chartered and approximate starting salary. And he said that depends on which company you are working with, but if I really want to have an indicator I should go – refer to the back of the magazines – of the engineering magazines where they have the salaries. And I said, oh that’s – the figures are too discouraging. And he said, I know, I don’t know what we did wrong, for all the professionals. So it’s a problem about salary in engineering and it’s – I like what I do but it’s quite a turn-off when I think of what I’m getting, what I will be getting, and what I could possibly get if I don’t work in engineering.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the placement experience will help you cope when you start work after graduation?

Subject:	Definitely. It’s – they don’t treat me very different from permanent so sometimes I have to consider myself a new graduate, apart from I’ll go back to uni life next year.

Interviewer:	Yes – are you looking forward to going back to uni?

Subject:	Yes and no. I am living on my own this year and I quite enjoy it, but you can’t really do that in Loughborough because that would be too expensive and I don’t really look forward to that. Um …

Interviewer:	Are you looking forward to doing the work?

Subject:	Yes and no. I forgot most of the things from what I learned in uni, like, um geotechnics and water, it’s something that I forgot straight away when I started.

Interviewer:	Yeah, you’re not the only person that’s said that.

Subject:	(inaudible)

Interviewer:	I’ve got some questions now that are questions that I asked in the last interview but it’s not a test to catch you out, it’s just to see if your opinion has changed with the experience that you’ve gained. I’m starting off with the hardest question as well. (OK) What five words would you use to describe the culture of your field of engineering? I mean that you’ve been working in?

Subject:	Mm… it’s analytical, it’s hard core, it’s, um, not well paid, it’s tough, um, it’s still quite masculine, yeah, and you tend to be more – something, um, something that I didn’t change my opinion is, it’s very different – engineering courses and art courses – for art courses you can have your own opinion and you can try to persuade people why you think that way and so on. With engineering it’s more a way to analyse and to reach the – to solve a problem – and it’s more, um, based on thinking than feelings.

Interviewer:	Do you think that that is just the way it’s always been or do you think that there could be more room for introducing more feelings and opinions?

Subject:	I think it’s always been and what it should be.

Interviewer:	Is that what appeals to you about it?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, I’m glad that it’s not too, all about feelings, like artistic, because, yeah I don’t think I’d like to work something like that. It’s nice but, yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think it is about engineering that makes it masculine?

Subject:	I’d say because girls are more, mm, they have more sensations, they’re more, what? I don’t know how to explain it but it’s about …

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s why what you just said about the arts versus engineering, why the arts tend to appeal more to women?

Subject:	Yeah, um, girls are more, um, they’re softer and they’ve got more feelings, are more sensitive. (Yeah) Some of them are described as less analytical and some of them will do things based on their feelings, but with engineering it’s the other side. You still do things based on your feelings but you’ve got to have the actual proof.

Interviewer:	Do you think that means that there’s maybe a certain type of girl that does engineering? Are there women that do engineering, would you say they’re like tomboys or less feminine or less girly girls or anything like that?

Subject:	They might be less girly girl. There wouldn’t be a lot of girls like [name] um, I do see a difference between girls in engineering and girls in other career. Um, it wouldn’t be for everybody but I’d say for most of the girls I met in engineering they are more, um, energetic type of person, um, they are more – they have stronger personalities, um, they do things – they – it seems like they always have a plan, that we’ll do this and this and this and in case that goes wrong we’ll do plan B and plan B2 and so on. And that’s why I found with girls in engineering. It could be the same for girls in other careers but I, from what I saw, it’s not as, um, what’s the word, visible.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	My high school lecturer she said, well there’s an advantage because for the sake of the company image they need you.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s true?

Subject:	Well, yes and no. I wouldn’t think that they do mind if you are girl or not, it’s a company that they’re going – they want to make money so if you are going to make money for them, no matter you are male or female or neither, they’re happy to take you. Um, sometimes as a girl they do help you out and they help you to carry heavy things, but there’s some blokes that they just run away, that happens, they leave you carrying everything else.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Yes and no. If other majors are encouraging people to do it then probably engineering should do the same, but I wouldn’t say encourage only women. It’s an open opportunity. If women feel that they’d like to work in engineering then they would go into it. Or possibly, um, I will know why they don’t like engineering, I’ve been told because they think it’s too difficult, they think it’s, it would be too analytical, something that they wouldn’t want to do when they have their career.

Interviewer:	Oh the other thing that I remembered that I was going to ask you was, have you moved, did you move to [town]?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Has that been, did you find that difficult or easy, moving somewhere?

Subject:	It’s, it was a bit difficult to get to know everything, but yeah, I’m quite easy to get used to things so, I’m quite lucky, and I live just next door to this company so it’s really close for me. When I say I want to travel the world a bit, sometimes it’s a bit – I’m not sure if I should do because I don’t know if I would get used to places as quickly as I do now, but yeah, I’ll see.

Interviewer:	OK, thank you very much, that’s everything.

Subject:	You’re welcome.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve just got a few questions about how the placement’s going and how it relates to your course and things like that, OK?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When did you start on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I started the 3rd of August.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s been going quite a while now then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Six months.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Can you tell me a bit about [company] and what they do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Company] is a multi-discipline engineering firm and they do transport, they do structural work, they do rail work, and geotechnics. They’ve got quite a few office in, elsewhere in UK and overseas.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s quite, um, open support – people are quite supportive and they’re willing to help you and share their experiences. That could be, um, different in different teams. I’m quite lucky that I worked in a team that people are really nice and friendly. Um, [company] got 12 key indicators and five, I don’t know what it’s called, five something that is customer obsessions, um, innovative, something, something. It basically tells you what the company wants you to achieve and everything, you know, it sounds like a promoter now. Um, yeah, it’s – they are quite focussed on customers. (Right, OK) I understand why, and they’ve got quite a few courses that they would like us to go on if we want to. They are always putting a huge amount of budget for training.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How useful do you think that the work that you’ve done on your degree has been to the work that you’re doing now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say 90% not relevant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not relevant?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because I’m doing transport, which is something that I didn’t expect that I would do. (Right) Um, um, what is useful that I’ve done in [university], it’s the way to approach the work and the way to analyse things. Um, so far what I’ve done is not very technical and I didn’t do any transport modules in [university], that’s why it’s not relevant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Is there anything that you wished you had learnt before you started the placement? Do you wish now that you had done transport modules or doesn’t it matter…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, well, it probably would be nice if I had, but I’d presume what you’ve learned in uni, it’s just a base to provide you with what, learning more actual practical knowledge. Um, so I think it’s OK that I didn’t do any transport.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, were you taught anything about health and safety at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it’s been highlighted when I was in uni but there wasn’t a specific course or guidelines because that varies from companies to companies, but they did make us know how important it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, so have you had health and safety training when you arrived here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh loads. Probably every – when I first started – probably every week, or there was a few courses in the same week, before they can let us go on site and do anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for coming on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it’s hard for me to say, because this is the only company that I have been working with. They’ve got guidelines of how to park in highways and everything. They could be different from other companies. So I think uni has done enough to make us know how important it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, before you started on placement did the university or your department say what they hoped you’d get out of doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They just said, make myself enjoy what I’m doing and, yeah, just an experience that, you know, the students who didn’t go on the placement wouldn’t get.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how have you found the transition from education to work, is it really easy or difficult?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I wouldn’t say difficult but certainly it’s very different. (Yes) Yeah. Um, there’s – every day I have to go to work and there’s no day off on Wednesdays. (OK) And, um, especially when I’m in traffic, I have to deal with the clients, authorities, myself, um, it’s not awfully technical but it could be quite difficult, and that’s not what we learned from uni. That’s real life and – yeah, real world.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you could have learned more inter-personal skills at uni or do you think it’s something that you develop through experience and that’s why doing a placement is a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I’d think that’d be learned as you work, because uni gives you a chance to do it but it would be different, they couldn’t pretend that they are clients and start shouting at you. (Yeah) Because people in uni are always nice and chilled out and relaxed and it’s not about profit and, and deadline and everything, so, yeah, it’s two different situations.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How do you think work and university do differ then? What do you think are the main differences?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, in uni we work and it’s about, we are going to, um, achieve a 2:1 or first grade and we are – as long as we’ve got the work done we can chill out and relax and do whatever we want. Um, well although we shouldn’t but I assume everybody did skip classes, well you can’t really do that at work and there’s more responsibility when you’re at work because you are issuing something, you are designing something, and people could have had a hard time if you’ve got a bad design and you could get yourself into troubles.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d say so. University, it’s more a short term goal, you can see yourself finishing in three, four, five years, but at work, that doesn’t get you a long way. If you are good and bright and you’ve got chances, probably five years you could be a manager but you can’t really vision the whole path.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What area are you working in here, is it transport?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Transport planning.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are there many women in your team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Both. Um, when I first started there was about eight men and three women including me. (OK) And now we’ve got five women, less male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Does the company have a structure or a programme in place for placement students to follow?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, what do you mean by that?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Maybe with specific targets and things that you should achieve throughout the year that you’re here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really, but they tend to provide you some help with your final year project and year out report. (OK) And they have, well we have appraisals, like other employees.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, you kind of have a scheme but it’s something everyone in the whole company does?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve heard that they’ve got sponsorships and other things but my manager didn’t mention it to me, so I don’t know if it varies from teams to teams or just my manager didn’t want to tell me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that it’d be a good idea if you had a specific programme to follow while you were here, or are you happy with the way things are going and what you’re doing at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It could be nice if there was a programme. Sometimes I feel that I’d like to have more feedbacks to know how I’m doing because I’m so new, and I don’t know what sort of work I should get out of it, um, and I’m quite lack of experiences because I’m totally new to transport. Um, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What does your actual job role involve then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, in transport planning there are safety studies, economic schemes, um, general planning, um, I’ve been working on safer routes to school, um, a safety scheme that is [motorway] Junction 18, um, I’ve been helping with [name] County Council it’s something about designing the pedestrian path for the whole area and I’m working on regional freight network, the south west, now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is that what you expected to be doing or were told to expect before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm. I was told that I would go out on sites probably once every week and now it depends, sometimes I got on site a few days in a row, sometimes I don’t get out in a whole month. It’s quite, well I’d say different, though I didn’t have a lot of expectation when I first started, again because I didn’t know what transport really is. It’s, um, I know that when, probably when you have more experience you’ll get to use the technical software like (Quadrow?) or (Oskadee?) and do safety schemes, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given the right level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm. I was chatting to a girl in my group. She used to work like a summer placement in the other office in [company] and she thinks that I have a lot more responsibility than she did, which is good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, OK, but even though you think you’ve got the right level of responsibility, do you feel that your team are supportive of you and if you do need help or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Extremely supportive, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How would you summarise your placement experience so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, there are ups and downs. Um, you feel quite good when you see a report issued with your name on it, but then you feel, oh, will they come back to me? And it’s – sometimes clients and the Government give you quite a hard time and they don’t, they could be fed up with work so they don’t speak really nicely and, yeah, but it’s a good experience that I know what the real world is and if I want to stay and work in England after I’ve graduated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that you will want to stay here when you’ve graduated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In [company] or in England?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Both.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, yes and no. I like the company, I like my team, but I’m not sure if transport is the right career for me. (OK) Sometimes I do still fancy working in structural, but on the other hand it seems quite boring in structural because for the whole, I don’t know, three, four or five months you’re calculating the same bridge or same project, but with transport you jump from here to there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s more varied?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You have different projects going on at the same time. So I might go and try out in structural later in April and see what I like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, within [company] they would maybe let you have that opportunity to …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, possibly go to the other floors and I’ll stay there for a few weeks.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, that’s good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. Um, as for England I don’t really know. It’s too expensive and engineering doesn’t give you what you’re worth. You work hard, you’ve got a lot of responsibility, you’ve got a lot to take from the clients and everyone, you’ve got a lot of work, but they don’t give you enough money and the taxes are quite heavy as well. (Yes) So it all depends on what the company offers me and I’ll also check the salaries for engineering in other countries.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that’s the biggest factor when you decide where to work or who is offering you the best package as it were rather than, I definitely want to go to this country or I definitely want to go to that country?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, both of them are important reasons. While they are offering you something, it could be – it depends on, oh how shall I explain it? They might offer you less but the cost of living there and having a better standard of life could be cheaper, so it depends. And there are some countries that I wouldn’t want to go, and also I, I’m planning to go to a country and stay there for a few years and then change to another, so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’d like to travel about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and that’s why I chose engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, because it’s something you can do everywhere?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s not similar to law or something like that that you have to stay.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that everything about doing a placement is good, or do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, in which aspect? Like drawback as in the fantasy is broken, or if I would do it again, or?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend that other people do a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I would. Um, you will be more competitive when you graduate and you could have contacts with companies and people, and you are not – you would be more, um, close to the real world. You are prepared for what you’re going to do when you’ve graduated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, they’re all the positive things. Do you think there are many disadvantages to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At the moment not really. Sometimes they tend to give me some easier work but I think no matter – probably because I’m placement or because I’ve no experience, so I think even though you’re a graduate, when you have no experience they’ll do the same. (OK) Oh, the only drawback is the salary. (Yes) It’s really, really bad!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that you have changed from doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Lots. Um, when I was in uni I thought I would like to do the MEng and I would like to work in the UK, and I wouldn’t mind to go to work on site. And I was only going to be either site engineer or structural engineer, and I thought I would choose no other career other than engineering, but now I’m not, I’m not sure if I will stay, if I will be site engineering, if I will stick with engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think there’s a possibility you might do something completely different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s possible.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think you’ll use what you’re learning now when you go back to your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I will. Um, in – study-wise there’s a module about highways that I think I should be more, having advantage over other course-mates, and my Excel skills that I learned here and, yeah, the way to organise things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. I know [name] is here but are there any other placement students at [company]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there are two other on my floor. One of them is from [university] as well and he, he was doing transport modules but he doesn’t work in transport planning, he works in [name]. I think that’s something to do with management. The other girl is, um, in the other team doing, oh I forgot what she does, but she did geography.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that it’s an advantage or a disadvantage having other placement students here, or don’t you have much to do with them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t have much to do with them. Mm. I just see them as other colleagues. (Yes) That, um, that’s as junior as I am.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel like you’re all treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yeah. Yeah. Sometimes we might have less chances to go on training courses because we are not (inaudible). I’ve been told that some of them couldn’t go on training courses because they are not permanent employee.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Is most of your work done in teams, or are you working a lot on your own?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I work quite a lot on my own, but because what I – for the current project that I’m doing it’s a project given to my colleague and he gave it to me, so whenever I’ve got problems I go back to him. That makes like a group work. And when we go out on sites normally we go out in pairs.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that doing teamwork at work compares to doing teamwork at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, in uni some of your course-mates can get quite irresponsible. I’m not saying my course because people in my course work fine, but when we work with some other courses, yeah. In here, um, they are quite determined and they are quite willing to, um, give the best output, so that’s something in common. And the group work in uni it’s – you tend to have the ideal situation, that something always works out, but in the real world there are more other factors that stops you and slow you down, and sometimes you, when you want to try to get some information, the other societies or parties will stop you or slow you down. So it’s not as fast as doing group work in uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that in the workplace individuals in a team maybe have a clearer role of what their job is than at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, possibly, yeah. Because again in uni when your group-mates don’t want to work, you’ve got to do what they want to do. Otherwise you just have a bad grade or, yeah, but in a company since all of them are quite willing to do something and they know what their role is, they know that if they don’t – response – they are not responsible for what they’re doing they’ll get into trouble as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Do you think that it’s worthwhile doing teamwork at university? Even though it’s different to teamwork in the workplace, do you think that you still learn things from it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. One of the reasons is there will be too much work if you work on your own, and it’s inter-personal skills that you get out of it from group work and you get to know your course-mate better as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. At work are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there are. They are nice people but they are just perfectionalist, it’s too hard to work with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Have you been given a mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, um, I’ve heard that a girl who is on placement as well, not from my floor, she has like a mentor, but we – well I just go and say something that I don’t like or like to my manager when I need, but he’s too busy, so I don’t always have the chance.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’d be a good idea to have a mentor then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, it might. It is not that only me who don’t have a mentor but I don’t think anybody in our team has a mentor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think would be the benefits of having a mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I could discuss more openly about, well, the packages or the possibilities of coming back after I graduate. Um, I’d say the career-wise would be clearer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there would be any drawbacks to having a mentor, or disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m not sure because I don’t have one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Is there anyone else apart from your line manager that you’ll go to for advice at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, my, my seniors. There are two, who are project managers, and one of them did my appraisal, so I’ll go and ask something if I want to know, but because he’s not yet a manager there are things that he doesn’t know yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. Is there anyone else in the company that you think of as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: As a role model?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In the company? My, um – the boss on my floor. He says that it was, there was a ball for the company and we were chatting, he said oh those few are star graduates, and my line manager thinks everybody in our team are outstanding, so I think basically everybody is doing a good job. And I know that my line manager’s quite hard-working and I look up to him, but I wouldn’t think that I would be as committed as he is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because I wouldn’t come in the office from half seven and leave at half six!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s like me! Has anyone from uni been to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – er, it’s [name of placement tutor].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Did you know him before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, he did, um, surveying in my second year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he tell you why he was visiting?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Because he was around [town]. That’s why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did he talk to you and your manager?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Well my manager was quite busy so they had a brief chat. (Right) And me – it was quite a long chat and because I knew him before, apart from what’s supposed to be passed on to me, we did some chit-chat and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of things was he asking you about the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He asked if everything’s going OK, um, and I just start telling him what I was doing, how I found this company, and he asked me what’s my career plan, my – the plan for my final year project and year out project, if I was planning to be chartered, what should I put in the portfolio, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Would you be happy to go to him if you had a problem with your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I would.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in contact with him or anyone else at uni the rest of the time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, not on a regular basis, but I do contact him a few times and the other tutor, [name], um, it was about the summer placement that I asked him and sometimes I contact with my friends in [university] but that’s not relevant really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know if either the university or here have a complaints procedure in place in case you did have any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well let me think. I don’t know about it in [university]. Here … we have the foreman ask us if we know about it, but we don’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about when you go out on site?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well that’s not enough facilities for both male and female really. They just stop along a trunk road, so yeah. But most of the time they’ve got things that we need.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And are there always women’s toilets on site and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really, but not for men either. (OK) So yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what about safety clothing and things like that, does that fit you or is it all in men’s sizes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well I’m happy because I’m not too small that I can fit in them. But I think [name] has a problem. They just don’t do smaller sizes in general. I think they can find it, but it’s just harder.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Can you think of any occasions when you feel like your gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people or the outcome of events?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm. Not really. I’d say because transport is not as hard core as structural, so – and they are not expecting there’s only male colleagues, so you get – you don’t really have the problem. And I’ve never heard [name] saying that she has a problem, so I suppose a consultancy would be more open.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah OK. Do you feel the same about that when you go on site as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because it’s me and my colleague. (Yeah) So they, they know me well and I know them well, and we work happily together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you have to deal with the labourers or anything like that at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, sometimes, not really. We might go and ask them a few questions, that’s not really labourers but they are someone who’s responsible for the local (inaudible) that’s going up and down on a road, even though it wasn’t me who was chatting to him it was my colleague, so I don’t feel any, like, discrimination.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK that’s good. We spoke earlier about your career and you thought that you don’t know whether you definitely want to go into engineering or not. Why do you think that you are considering not going into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s again salary. (Yeah) Um, I was thinking, if I stay in England I might consider alternatives, or might – it could be other companies. I’m not sure how much in general this career is offering, but sometimes I feel like I should get more for what I do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you thought about what you might do instead?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Accounting. Yeah, possible. Or go into Government.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. If you did stay in engineering, do you think that you’d like a more managerial role or would you like to go down the technical or specialist route?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I used to think that I would be working in management side, but from seeing what my managers do I don’t think that’s very interesting. He has meetings, actual, actually every day, or sometimes two or three meetings in a day, and when I say sometimes customers or clients shout at us, I think he got even more than we do because he’s dealing with all of them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed from doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah, lots. Um, as I said I used to have all the goals that I thought I would like to achieve. Now I would think again and some of them has changed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the placement will help you when you do start work? Even if you go into something completely different do you think the experience will still be helpful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it would. There was, um, someone who came for an interview and she is a Masters student but because she has no, um, experience, I’m not sure if they’re going to take her but it sounds not very, um, it’s not someone that they would like to have, with no experience. And again, if I go into different fields, there are skills that I learned here that will, that could be applied there and wouldn’t learn there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – things like dealing with clients and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, if [company] offered you a job, would you come and work for them when you’ve finished uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Possibly, it depends on how much they are offering. I need to talk about money now! There was once – I went to a career fair, it was a few months ago in [airport], and I had a chat with the IStructE, the executive, and I can’t remember what he was but I think he’s the chief executive of IStructE, and I asked him about the salary, before and after chartered and approximate starting salary. And he said that depends on which company you are working with, but if I really want to have an indicator I should go – refer to the back of the magazines – of the engineering magazines where they have the salaries. And I said, oh that’s – the figures are too discouraging. And he said, I know, I don’t know what we did wrong, for all the professionals. So it’s a problem about salary in engineering and it’s – I like what I do but it’s quite a turn-off when I think of what I’m getting, what I will be getting, and what I could possibly get if I don’t work in engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the placement experience will help you cope when you start work after graduation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. It’s – they don’t treat me very different from permanent so sometimes I have to consider myself a new graduate, apart from I’ll go back to uni life next year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes – are you looking forward to going back to uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and no. I am living on my own this year and I quite enjoy it, but you can’t really do that in Loughborough because that would be too expensive and I don’t really look forward to that. Um …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you looking forward to doing the work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and no. I forgot most of the things from what I learned in uni, like, um geotechnics and water, it’s something that I forgot straight away when I started.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, you’re not the only person that’s said that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (inaudible)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve got some questions now that are questions that I asked in the last interview but it’s not a test to catch you out, it’s just to see if your opinion has changed with the experience that you’ve gained. I’m starting off with the hardest question as well. (OK) What five words would you use to describe the culture of your field of engineering? I mean that you’ve been working in?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm… it’s analytical, it’s hard core, it’s, um, not well paid, it’s tough, um, it’s still quite masculine, yeah, and you tend to be more – something, um, something that I didn’t change my opinion is, it’s very different – engineering courses and art courses – for art courses you can have your own opinion and you can try to persuade people why you think that way and so on. With engineering it’s more a way to analyse and to reach the – to solve a problem – and it’s more, um, based on thinking than feelings.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that that is just the way it’s always been or do you think that there could be more room for introducing more feelings and opinions?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s always been and what it should be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what appeals to you about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, I’m glad that it’s not too, all about feelings, like artistic, because, yeah I don’t think I’d like to work something like that. It’s nice but, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think it is about engineering that makes it masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d say because girls are more, mm, they have more sensations, they’re more, what? I don’t know how to explain it but it’s about …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s why what you just said about the arts versus engineering, why the arts tend to appeal more to women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, um, girls are more, um, they’re softer and they’ve got more feelings, are more sensitive. (Yeah) Some of them are described as less analytical and some of them will do things based on their feelings, but with engineering it’s the other side. You still do things based on your feelings but you’ve got to have the actual proof.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that means that there’s maybe a certain type of girl that does engineering? Are there women that do engineering, would you say they’re like tomboys or less feminine or less girly girls or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They might be less girly girl. There wouldn’t be a lot of girls like [name] um, I do see a difference between girls in engineering and girls in other career. Um, it wouldn’t be for everybody but I’d say for most of the girls I met in engineering they are more, um, energetic type of person, um, they are more – they have stronger personalities, um, they do things – they – it seems like they always have a plan, that we’ll do this and this and this and in case that goes wrong we’ll do plan B and plan B2 and so on. And that’s why I found with girls in engineering. It could be the same for girls in other careers but I, from what I saw, it’s not as, um, what’s the word, visible.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My high school lecturer she said, well there’s an advantage because for the sake of the company image they need you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s true?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, yes and no. I wouldn’t think that they do mind if you are girl or not, it’s a company that they’re going – they want to make money so if you are going to make money for them, no matter you are male or female or neither, they’re happy to take you. Um, sometimes as a girl they do help you out and they help you to carry heavy things, but there’s some blokes that they just run away, that happens, they leave you carrying everything else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes and no. If other majors are encouraging people to do it then probably engineering should do the same, but I wouldn’t say encourage only women. It’s an open opportunity. If women feel that they’d like to work in engineering then they would go into it. Or possibly, um, I will know why they don’t like engineering, I’ve been told because they think it’s too difficult, they think it’s, it would be too analytical, something that they wouldn’t want to do when they have their career.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh the other thing that I remembered that I was going to ask you was, have you moved, did you move to [town]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that been, did you find that difficult or easy, moving somewhere?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s, it was a bit difficult to get to know everything, but yeah, I’m quite easy to get used to things so, I’m quite lucky, and I live just next door to this company so it’s really close for me. When I say I want to travel the world a bit, sometimes it’s a bit – I’m not sure if I should do because I don’t know if I would get used to places as quickly as I do now, but yeah, I’ll see.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, thank you very much, that’s everything.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You’re welcome.
